title: An engagement invitation for your kind of promise
excerpt: Keep the first announcement personal, explain the gathering clearly, and let a few well-chosen words carry the excitement.

sections.heading: Name the moment in your own words
paragraphs: An engagement may be an intimate meal, a ring exchange, or a larger family celebration. Name the gathering in the way that makes sense to you. Guests should understand what they are being invited to without needing to know every family custom.

You can be joyful without writing a grand speech. Put the couple’s names near a short opening, then let the date and venue follow. A line such as ‘A little promise, a lifetime ahead’ works as a cover; the message below can explain the occasion more directly.
sections.quote: Please join us as we celebrate our engagement with the people closest to our hearts. We would love to begin this chapter with you.

sections.heading: Help guests picture the gathering
paragraphs: Tell guests whether the invitation includes a meal and whether there is a particular arrival time. If an exchange or announcement is planned, give that its own schedule item. There is no need to invent a programme for a relaxed gathering; one clear entry can be enough.

Use a complete address, including the floor or hall when useful. For a gathering at home, include the building entrance or parking note you would normally send in a separate message. Keep any personal instructions appropriate to the people who will receive the link.
list: Check both names and any family acknowledgements.
Include the correct day, date, time and timezone.
Explain whether guests should arrive before a particular moment.
Provide directions and a clear way to respond.

sections.heading: Choose a voice you can keep
paragraphs: Formal wording can sit beside a warm closing, and a bilingual line can feel completely natural. Keep one idea per sentence so the invitation remains easy to read on a small phone. Every suggested line is a starting point, not something you have to preserve.

Preview the invitation with your real names before choosing a design. Longer names need breathing room, especially beside ornate artwork. Finish by checking that your invitation still sounds like the people hosting it.
